en: The Extensive Treatise on the Five Aggregates of the Mahāyāna, in one fascicle.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Sthiramati;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śīlabhadra of Central India during the Great Tang Dynasty.

Translated by Imperial Decree. The Buddha taught the five aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ*): namely, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
What is the aggregate of form?
This refers to the four great elements and the matter derived from the great elements.
What are the four great elements?
They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
What, then, are these? They are the solid nature of earth, the moist nature of water, the warm nature of fire, and the light nature of wind.
As for "element" (*dhātu*), it is so called because it maintains its own intrinsic nature as well as the derived matter produced from it.
What is derived matter from the four great elements?

It refers to the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty; visible form, sound, odor, taste, and a portion of tangible objects; as well as non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), and so forth.
The meaning of "creator" (*kartṛ*) is the sense of cause.
The meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*) is the sense of being most excellent and sovereign, the sense of mastery, and the sense of predominance; this is the meaning of "faculty.
As for the phrase "the sense of mastery," with whom does it exercise mastery?
This means that the eye faculty and the eye-consciousness act as the primary conditions for the arising of eye-consciousness.
In this manner, it continues up to the body faculty and the body-consciousness acting as the primary conditions for the arising of body-consciousness.
What is the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*)?
It takes visible form as its object and has translucent matter as its nature.
That is to say, it is a portion of translucent matter within the eye, like clarified butter; because this nature exists, visual consciousness arises, and in its absence, it does not arise.
What is the ear faculty (*śrotra-indriya*)?
It takes sound as its object and has pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) as its nature.
This refers to a portion of pure matter within the ear; because this nature exists, auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) arises, and in its absence, it does not arise.
What is the nose faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*)?
It has fragrance as its object and pure matter (*rūpaprasāda*) as its nature.
That is to say, it is a portion of pure matter within the nose; because this nature exists, nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*) arises, and in its absence, it does not arise.
What is the tongue faculty (*jihvendriya*)?
It has taste as its object and pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) as its nature.

This refers to the pure matter that pervades the entire tongue; some say there is a small portion on the tongue that does not pervade it, such as the tip of a hair. Because this nature exists, tongue-consciousness (*jihvāvijñāna*) arises; if it were absent, it would not arise.
What is the body faculty (*kāyendriya*)?
It has tangibles as its object and pure matter (*rūpaprasāda*) as its intrinsic nature.
This refers to the pervasive pure matter within the body; because this nature exists, body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) arises, and in its absence, it does not arise.
What is form (*rūpa*)?
It refers to the objective domain of the eye, including manifest color (*varṇa-rūpa*), shape (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), and informative form (*vijñapti-rūpa*).
Manifest color is of four kinds: namely, blue, yellow, red, and white.
Visible form refers to length, shortness, and so forth.
What is sound?
It refers to the object of the ear: sound caused by appropriated primary elements, sound caused by non-appropriated primary elements, and sound caused by both types of primary elements.
All minds and mental factors are the appropriators (*upādātṛ*), while sentient beings are the appropriated (*upādāna*).
Regarding sound caused by the great elements as the basis of appropriation: this refers to sounds such as those produced when hands strike one another or the sounds of speech.
Sound caused by non-appropriated primary elements (*mahābhūta*) refers, for example, to the sounds of wind, forests, or rushing water.
Sound caused by both [appropriated and non-appropriated] primary elements refers, for example, to the sound of a hand striking a drum.
What is odor? It refers to the object of the nose: pleasant odors, unpleasant odors, and neutral odors.
Pleasant odors are those which, when they come into contact with the nose, provide benefit to the continuity of the aggregates.
Unpleasant odor refers to that which, upon contact with the nose, causes harm or impairment to the continuity of the aggregates.
Neutral odor refers to that which, upon contact with the nose, neither causes harm nor provides benefit.
What is taste?
It refers to the objects of the tongue: sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, bland, and so forth.
What is a portion of the tangible?
This refers to the objects of the body, excluding the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), namely: smoothness, roughness, heaviness, lightness, cold, hunger, thirst, and so forth.
Smoothness means being fine and soft; roughness means being coarse and hard; heaviness means being weighable; lightness means the opposite.
When heat desires to become cold, touch is the cause of that cold; this is a case of designating the effect by the name of its cause.

It is as when it is said: "The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is blissful; the preaching of the True Dharma is blissful; the harmony of the Saṅgha is blissful; and practicing diligence together is blissful."
Although diligent exertion and arduous effort are causes of happiness, they are themselves described as happiness.
This case is likewise: the desire to eat is hunger, and the desire to drink is thirst; the description is the same.
The seven kinds of derivative tangible objects (*upādāyarūpa*) along with the aforementioned four great elements (*mahābhūta*), totaling eleven types, have already been explained.
What, then, are non-informative matter (*avijñaptirūpa*) and so forth?
They are the invisible and non-obstructive matter (*anidarśana-apratigha-rūpa*) produced by informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) refers to bodily and vocal informative action; this is categorized as wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
"The matter produced" refers to the matter that arises precisely from those wholesome or unwholesome informative actions.
This cannot be manifested, and is therefore called "unmanifest" (avijñapti).
That which is "matter produced by samādhi" refers to the matter produced by the four dhyānas and so forth.
This unmanifest matter is of a derivative nature; it is termed "virtuous restraint," "non-virtuous restraint," and so on, and is also called "karma" and "seed."
Such forms, in brief, are of three kinds:
first, those that are visible and resistant; second, those that are invisible and resistant; and third, those that are invisible and non-resistant.
Among these, that which is visible and resistant refers to visible form (*varṇa*) and so forth;
that which is invisible and resistant refers to the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and so forth;
and that which is invisible and non-resistant refers to unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and so forth.
What is the aggregate of feeling?
There are three kinds of feeling: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Pleasant feeling refers to that which, at the time of its cessation, gives rise to a desire for reunion.
Painful feeling refers to that which, when it arises, involves the desire for separation.
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling refers to the absence of both desires.
The absence of both desires means the absence of the desire for union and the desire for separation.
Feeling (*vedanā*) refers to the consciousness’s experiencing.
What is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*)?
It is that which is capable of preeminently grasping the characteristics of various objects.
"Superior grasping" refers to the capacity for superior power to grasp.
Just as one who possesses great strength is called "one of superior strength," so it is here.
What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)?
This refers to all other mental factors (*caitasika*) and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*), excluding feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).
What are the other mental factors?
They are those formations that are associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*).

Contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), volition (*cetanā*); desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*); faith (*śraddhā*), shame (*hrī*), dread (*apatrāpya*), non-attachment (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adveṣa*), non-delusion (*amoha*), diligence (*vīrya*), pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), non-harming (*ahiṃsā*); attachment (*lobha*), hatred (*dveṣa*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*); anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), vexation (*pradāsa*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), deceit (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), arrogance (*mada*), harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*); lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), heedlessness (*pramāda*), forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), distraction (*vikṣepa*), lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*); regret (*kaukṛtya*), sleep (*middha*), applied thought (*vitarka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
Among these mental factors, five are universal (*sarvatraga*).
They are called universal because they pervade all wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate minds.
Five are object-specific (*viniyata*).
Each of these five categories, with respect to their distinct objects, is mutually determined and inseparable; thus, where one exists, all must exist.
Eleven are wholesome, six are afflictions (*kleśa*), the remainder are secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and four are indeterminate (*aniyata*).
These four indeterminate factors are not primary secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), because they pertain to both the wholesome and the neutral (*avyākṛta*) natures.
The essential nature and function of contact (*sparśa*) and the others should now be explained.
What is contact (*sparśa*)?
It is the conjunction of the three, having discernment as its essential nature.
The "conjunction of the three" refers to the eye, visible form, consciousness, and so forth.
The conjunction of these factors gives rise to the mind and mental states; therefore, it is called contact (*sparśa*).
Its function is to serve as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*).
What is attention (*manasikāra*)?
Its nature is that which causes the mind to awaken;
its meaning is that which brings mental states and mental factors into manifestation and rouses them.
Its function is to sustain the mind as it takes an object.
What is volition (*cetanā*)?
It is that which causes the mind to engage with virtues, faults, or that which is neither;
its nature is mental action (*manas-karman*).

If this nature exists, the cognitive function of apprehending objects immediately manifests before one; just as a magnet attracts iron and causes it to move, its activity consists in impelling the mind toward the wholesome, the unwholesome, or the indeterminate.
What is desire (*chanda*)?
It is characterized by the longing for objects that are pleasing and desirable.
"Pleasing and desirable objects" refers to things such as those one wishes to see or hear; it carries the sense of wishing for, delighting in, and seeking after them.
Its function is to serve as the basis for diligence.
What is resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*)?
It is defined as the act of assenting to a determined object exactly as it has been cognized.
Regarding the "definitive object," this refers to the five aggregates and so forth, as the Kinsman of the Sun (the Buddha) has taught:
form is like a mass of foam, feeling is like a water bubble, perception is like a mirage, mental formations are like a plantain tree, and consciousness is like a magical illusion.
It is thus determined.
Or, it is as the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) in which various phenomena abide; that is to say, it arises as such a determination.
What is called "determination" (niścaya) has the meaning of "sealing and upholding" (mudrā-dhāraṇa).
The others have no capacity to project or lead [to rebirth], for this [volition] is preeminent and cannot be projected by anything else.
What is mindfulness?
It is the non-forgetting of a familiar object by the mind, having clear recollection as its essential nature.
Regarding "habitual practice," this refers to that which has been previously practiced and performed.
Its function is to serve as the basis for non-distraction. What is samādhi?
It refers to one-pointedness of mind regarding the object of observation.
The "object of observation" refers to the five aggregates and so forth, as well as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, selflessness, and so on.
"One-pointedness of mind" has the meaning of focused concentration.
Its function is to serve as the basis for wisdom.
Because the mind is concentrated, one understands things as they truly are.
What is wisdom?

This refers to that which has the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) as its intrinsic nature; it is either induced by correct reasoning, induced by incorrect reasoning, or induced by neither.
"That which refers to that" means the object under investigation.

The discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) refers to the attainment of certainty through the analytical investigation of the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena by means of wisdom.
Those "led by what is reasoned" (*yoniśomanasikāra-niṣpanna*) refer to the disciples of the Buddha.
That which is induced by what is not in accordance with reason refers to the various non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
That which is induced by neither refers to other sentient beings.
Its function is to sever doubt.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) is that which discriminates, for it attains certainty regarding all phenomena.
What is faith (*śraddhā*)?
It is defined as a state of mental purity characterized by profound and correct conformity toward karma, its results, the [Four] Truths, and the [Three] Jewels.
Regarding action, it refers to meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable karma.
Regarding fruit, it refers to the fruits of stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and arhatship.
Regarding the truths, they refer to the truths of suffering, origination, cessation, and the path.
Regarding the jewels, they refer to the Jewels of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
To be in complete accord with such [teachings] as karma and its results is also termed "purity" and has the sense of "aspiration."
Its function is to serve as the basis for the granting of consent.
What is shame (*hrī*)?
It is defined as having the nature of feeling abashed regarding committed transgressions, based on oneself and based on the Dharma.
"Fault" (*āpatti*) refers to transgression, for it is that which the wise loathe and dread.
"Moral shame" (*hrī*) refers to the non-commission of various misdeeds;
its function is to serve as the basis for the prevention and cessation of unwholesome conduct.
What is shame (*hrī*)?
It is defined as having the nature of feeling abashed regarding the misdeeds one has committed, with others as the predominant influence.
"With others as the predominant influence" means feeling shame before others regarding all faults and transgressions out of fear of punishment, censure, and so forth.
Karma is as explained under "shame" (*hrī*).
What is non-attachment (*alobha*)?
It is the antidote to attachment; its nature is to cause deep revulsion and to be free from clinging.
Attachment to various states of existence (*bhava*) and the requisites for existence is called greed; its antidote is said to be non-greed.

This refers to the meaning of being free from attachment to existence and its requisites. Because it involves the thorough knowledge of all the faults of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), it is termed "revulsion" (*nirvid*).
Its function is to serve as the basis for the non-arising of unwholesome conduct.
What is non-hatred?
It is the antidote to hatred, having loving-kindness (*maitrī*) as its essential nature.
It means the sense of not harming sentient beings.
Karma is as explained in the case of non-attachment (*alobha*).
What is non-delusion (*amoha*)?
This refers to the antidote to delusion, having the nature of correct practice according to reality.
"According to reality" means, in brief, the Four Noble Truths; in detail, the twelve links of dependent origination. To apply oneself to these is the meaning of right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).
Karma is also explained as [the absence of] non-attachment.
What is diligence?
It is the antidote to laziness, having the nature of energetic exertion directed toward the presence of wholesome qualities.
This means: whether it be donning the armor, or the preparatory application, or being free from cowardice, or being non-regressive, or being free from complacency—such is its meaning.
Its function is the complete accomplishment of wholesome dharmas.
What is pliancy (*praśrabdhi*)?
It is the antidote to heaviness and rigidity (*dausthulya*); its nature is the fitness and flexibility of body and mind, which enables one to abandon the ten unwholesome courses of action.
Its function is the removal of hindrances.
By the power of this, all obstacles are eliminated and the heavy burdens (*dauṣṭhulya*) are discarded.
What is heedfulness (*apramāda*)?
It is the antidote to heedlessness; relying on non-attachment up to diligence, it consists in abandoning all unwholesome states and cultivating their wholesome antidotes.
Laxity (*pramāda*) refers to greed, hatred, delusion, and indolence; non-laxity (*apramāda*) is that which serves as their antidote.
This means relying upon the four factors of non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, and diligence to counteract unwholesome states and cultivate wholesome states.
Its function is to serve as the basis for correct practice, both mundane and supramundane.
What is equanimity?
It refers to the attainment of mental evenness, mental rectitude, and mental effortlessness, based upon such non-attachment, non-hatred, and so forth, up to diligence.
Furthermore, by means of this, one becomes free from all defiled phenomena and dwells in pure phenomena.

That is to say, by relying on the nature of non-attachment, non-hatred, non-delusion, and diligence, or by occasionally distancing oneself from the faults of lethargy and agitation, one first attains equanimity of mind;
or, by occasionally proceeding spontaneously without exertion, one subsequently attains rectitude of mind.
At times, because one is far removed from all defilements, one ultimately attains a state of mind that is effortless (*anābhoga*).
This karma is as explained in the section on heedfulness (*apramāda*).
What is non-harming (*avihiṃsā*)?
It refers to the antidote to harming, having compassion as its essential nature.
Because of compassion, one does not harm living beings; this is a portion of non-hatred.
Its function is to refrain from injuring or afflicting others.
What is craving?
It is characterized by defiled attachment and clinging toward the five aggregates of grasping.
Bound by this fetter, one transmigrates through the three realms.
Its function is to produce suffering.
By the power of craving, the five aggregates of clinging are produced.
What is aversion?
It is defined as having the nature of harming sentient beings.
Its function is to serve as the basis for dwelling in insecurity and for engaging in unwholesome conduct.
"Insecurity" refers to the fact that by harming others, one dwells in suffering oneself.
What is pride?

There are seven kinds of pride: namely, pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*adhimāna*), pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), the pride of self (*asmimāna*), overweening pride (*abhimāna*), inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*), and false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
What is pride (*māna*)?
It is the nature of mental loftiness that consists in considering oneself superior to those who are inferior, or considering oneself equal to those who are one's equals.
What is excessive pride (*atimāna*)?
That is to say, it is the nature of the mind being uplifted when one considers oneself superior to those who are equal, or considers oneself equal to those who are superior.
What is excessive pride (*atimāna*)?
It is the nature of the mind being uplifted when one considers oneself superior to those who are actually superior.
What is the conceit of self (*asmimāna*)?
It refers to the nature of mental exaltation that arises from reckoning the five aggregates of clinging as "I" or "mine.
What is overweening conceit (*adhimāna*)?
It refers to the nature of mental inflation that thinks, "I have attained" those superior and distinguished dharmas of realization which one has not yet attained.
"Superior and distinguished dharmas of realization" refers to the fruits of the noble ones (*āryaphala*), as well as *samādhi*, *samāpatti*, and so forth.
To claim "I have attained" that which one has not yet attained, and thereby become arrogant—this is called pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*).
What is pride of inferiority?
It is the nature of mental exaltation that, regarding those who are largely superior, one reckons oneself to be slightly inferior.
What is false pride (*mithyāmāna*)?
It is the nature of a mind that is loftily uplifted by conceiving oneself to possess virtues when one actually lacks them.
Its function is to serve as a basis for the failure to give rise to reverence.
It refers to giving rise to arrogance toward one's elders and those of virtuous qualities, and failing to cultivate reverence for them.
What is ignorance (*avidyā*)?
It is characterized by a lack of wisdom regarding karma, its results, the [Four] Truths, and the [Three] Jewels.
This is of two kinds:
first, innate (*sahaja*); second, conceptual (*vikalpita*).

Furthermore, greed, hatred, and ignorance in the desire realm constitute the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*), namely: the unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion.
Furthermore, these arise either simultaneously, not simultaneously, or through conceptual construction.
Those that arise simultaneously refer to [afflictions] such as those of birds and beasts.
Those that do not arise simultaneously refer to [afflictions] associated with greed and so forth.
Discrimination refers to that which is associated with various views and involves false certitude.
Its function is to serve as the basis for the affliction of doubt.
What are views?

There are five kinds of views: namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
What is the view of a self-identity?
This refers to the nature of defiled wisdom that adheres to the five aggregates of clinging as either "I" or "mine.
*Sat* means the sense of "perishing," and *kāya* means the sense of "aggregation" or "accumulation. Thus, it is the perishable collection (*sat-kāya*).
Within this very context, one perceives a self as permanent, distinct from the aggregates, and regards the aggregates as "mine" and so forth.
For what reason, then, is it further stated that "sat" (being) destroys the notion of permanence and "kāya" (body) destroys the notion of unity?
It is an impermanent accumulation because within it there is no self (*ātman*) nor what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*).
"Defiled wisdom" refers to that which coexists with the afflictions (*kleśa*);
its function is to serve as the basis for all categories of views (*dṛṣṭi-gaṇa*).
What is the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)?
It is, by the predominant power of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the grasping of that which is apprehended as either eternal or annihilated; its nature is defiled wisdom.
The extreme of permanence refers to the adherence to a self that is sovereign, pervasive, eternal, and so forth.

The extreme of annihilation refers to the adherence to an agent such as a "puruṣa" (person), holding that after death one is not reborn, just as a jar, once broken, can no longer serve its purpose of containing things.
Its function is to obstruct the departure via the Middle Way.
What is wrong view?
It refers to the denial of cause and effect, or the denial of functional efficacy, or the subversion of wholesome things; its intrinsic nature is defiled wisdom.
Regarding the denial of causes: "causes" refers to the nature of karma and afflictions, which together comprise five branches.
There are three types of afflictions, namely: ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*).
Karma is of two kinds, namely: formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*).
"Existence" refers to the seeds of various karmas based upon the ālayavijñāna; this too is called karma.
As the Blessed One said:
"Ānanda! If karma can produce a fruit in the future, that too is called 'existent'.
Such statements as these constitute the denial known as "denial of the cause."

Regarding the denial of the fruit: the fruit consists of seven members, namely consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, birth, and old age and death; to deny these is to deny the fruit.

Furthermore, to deny the existence of wholesome and unwholesome actions is called "denying the cause"; to deny the existence of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome actions is called "denying the fruit.
To deny this world and the next, to deny the existence of father and mother, and to deny the existence of beings born by transformation—these denials constitute "denying function."
This refers to the activity of migrating from this world to another world, the activity of maintaining the seeds [of existence], the activity of linking rebirth, and so forth.
To deny the existence of arhats in this world and so on is to destroy wholesome deeds.
Its function is to sever the roots of goodness.
Its function is to serve as the firm basis for the unwholesome roots.
Furthermore, its function is to give rise to the unwholesome and prevent the arising of the wholesome.
What is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)?

It refers to the defiled wisdom that, with respect to the three views and the aggregates upon which they depend, reckons them as supreme, foremost, excellent, and ultimate; its intrinsic nature is such defiled wisdom.
The three views refer to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The aggregates that serve as their basis are those very aggregates upon which these views depend.
Their karma is as explained in the section on false view.
What is the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?
It refers to the nature of defiled wisdom that, with respect to precepts, observances, and the aggregates upon which they depend, reckons them as being purification, liberation, or transcendence.
"Precept" (*śīla*) refers to abstaining from the seven types of evil preceded by wrong views.

"Vow" (*vratā*) refers to the vows of the cow-herders, dog-herders, and so forth, as well as practices such as plucking out one's hair, carrying the triple staff, or the *sāṃkhya* system’s meditative concentration and wisdom; these are not causes for liberation.
Furthermore, they reckon Maheśvara or the World-Lord (Lokapāla), as well as entering fire and water and so forth, to be the causes for rebirth in heaven;
such things as these they reckon to be the cause.
The "aggregates that serve as the basis" refer to the very aggregates upon which the observance of precepts and prohibitions depend.
"Purity" refers to explaining these uninterrupted skillful means as being purity itself.
"Liberation" means that by means of this very [path], one is liberated from the afflictions.
"Departure" means that by means of this very [path], one departs from birth and death. Such is the meaning.
Its function is to serve as the basis for fruitlessness, futility, and weariness.
"Fruitlessness and futility" means that this [state] cannot achieve the sense of escaping from suffering.
What is doubt?
It refers to the nature of hesitation regarding whether the truths, the jewels, and so forth, exist or do not exist;
its function is to serve as the basis for the non-arising of wholesome dharmas.

Among the various afflictions (*kleśa*), the last three views (*dṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) arise solely through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpita*); the remaining ones pertain to both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptually discriminated arising.
What is anger (*krodha*)?
It is defined as having the nature of mental indignation based on a presently manifest harmful object.
Its function is to provide a basis for those who are violent and wicked to wield whips and staves.
What is resentment (*upanāha*)?
It is characterized by the nature of harboring a grudge without relinquishing it, preceded by anger (*krodha*).
Its function is to serve as the basis for intolerance.
What is concealment (*mrakṣa*)?
It has the nature of hiding one's faults; that is, it consists in the concealment of transgressions.
When he is being instructed, he is unable to confess his fault; this is a portion of delusion (*moha*).
Its function is to serve as the basis for remorse and a lack of abiding in peace.
What is resentment (*pradāsa*)?
It is defined as having the nature of uttering violent and malicious speech and of being offensive and intrusive.
Preceded by anger and resentment, it gives rise to a mind intent on causing harm.
"Violent and malicious speech" refers to words that are cutting, harmful, and coarse; its function is to serve as the basis for sorrow, suffering, and a lack of peaceful dwelling.
Furthermore, it has the function of producing non-merit and the function of giving rise to an evil reputation.
What is envy (*īrṣyā*)?
It is characterized by a mind of malice toward the prosperity of others.
For the sake of fame and profit, one is unable to endure the prosperity of others, and a mind of envy arises.
Its function is to serve as a basis for one's own dwelling in sorrow and suffering.
What is stinginess?
It is that which is contrary to giving, having the nature of a stingy mind.
Because one gives rise to a sense of parsimony toward wealth and other things, one is unable to practice generosity; such is stinginess (*mātsarya*).
It is the mind’s pervasive attachment to gains and requisites, and it is a derivative of greed (*lobha*).
Its function is to serve as the basis for lack of contentment.
As for "lack of contentment," due to stinginess, one constantly accumulates even those things that are not being used.
What is deception?
It is defined as having the nature of falsely manifesting unreal virtues to others through deceit.
It is a derivative of greed (*lobha*) and functions as the basis for wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
What is guile (*śāṭhya*)?
It is defined as the nature of mental crookedness that employs deceptive expedients to conceal one's own faults and evils;
it consists of being attached to fame and profit, and is a derivative of greed and delusion.
Its function is to obstruct correct instruction.
Furthermore, because it is accompanied by fault, one does not truthfully disclose and repent, and thus is unfit for instruction.
What is pride (*māna*)?
It refers to having the nature of being able to exhaustively [overcome] attachment and arrogance regarding flourishing circumstances.
"Flourishing circumstances" refers to contaminated (sāsrava) flourishing circumstances.
"Attachment and arrogance" refers to being enamored with, delighted by, and taking pride in such things; it is a portion of greed (*lobha*).
"Capable of exhausting" means that this is capable of exhausting all roots of goodness.
What is "harming"?
It has the nature of inflicting injury and affliction upon sentient beings; it is a derivative of hatred (*dveṣa*).
"Inflicting harm" refers to applying such things as whips and staves;
its function is to serve as the basis for this [harm].
What is lack of shame (*āhrīkya*)?
It is defined as having the nature of not feeling shame for the misdeeds one has committed.
Its function is to act as an associate to all primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
What is lack of dread (*āhrīkya*)?
It is defined as having the nature of not feeling shame before others regarding the misdeeds one has committed.
Its function is as explained for *āhrīkya* (lack of self-respect).
What is *styāna* (sloth)?
It refers to the mind being unrefined and lacking capability, having delusion as its essential nature; it is a derivative of ignorance.
Its function is to serve as the basis for all primary afflictions and secondary afflictions.
What is restlessness (*auddhatya*)?
It is characterized by a lack of mental tranquility resulting from recollecting matters such as joy and pleasure.
One should understand that the lack of mental tranquility arising from recollecting past instances of play, laughter, and the like is a derivative of craving (*rāga*).
Its function is to obstruct *śamatha*.
What is lack of faith (*āśraddhya*)?
It is the antithesis of faith; its nature is a lack of pure clarity of mind due to a failure to have correct faith and conviction in the results of karma and so forth.
Its function is to serve as the basis for indolence.
What is indolence?
It is defined as that which is the antithesis of diligence; its essential nature is a lack of mental vigor regarding all categories of wholesome qualities.
Its function is to obstruct the diligent cultivation of various virtues.
What is heedlessness?
It is characterized by the failure to guard the mind against the afflictions and the inability to cultivate virtuous qualities, due to reliance on greed, hatred, delusion, and laziness.
Its function is to serve as the basis for the increase of unwholesome states and the decline of wholesome dharmas.
What is loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*)?
It refers to defiled mindfulness, characterized by the inability to clearly remember various wholesome dharmas.
Defiled mindfulness refers to that which is associated with the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding "lack of clarity concerning the wholesome," this means being unable to retain the meaning of the correct instructions.
Its function is to serve as a basis for distraction (*vikṣepa*).
What is distraction (*vikṣepa*)?
It is a derivative of greed, hatred, and delusion, characterized by causing the mind and mental factors to flow and disperse.
Its function is to obstruct freedom from desire (*vairāgya*).
What is lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*)?
It is wisdom associated with the afflictions, having as its nature the ability to give rise to improper conduct of body, speech, and mind.
Its function is to serve as the basis for violating the rules of discipline (*vinaya*).

This refers to failing to correctly examine the past, future, and so forth, whereby one is unable to discern what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, resulting in the violation of the code of discipline.
What is *kaukṛtya* (remorse/wrongdoing)?
It has the nature of mental regret and remorse.
It is called "bad conduct" (*kaukṛtya*) because it pertains to what was poorly done.
The essence of this bad conduct is not the regret itself; rather, it is so named because a subsequent remorse arises following a prior act of misconduct.
This is designated as "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*) by referring to the effect through its cause;
it is, for example, like the six bases of contact being called "prior karma.
This has two aspects, namely: wholesome and unwholesome.
Within these two states, there are again two types each.
If, within the state of the wholesome, one first fails to perform a wholesome deed and subsequently gives rise to a mind of regret, that cause is wholesome, and the regret is likewise wholesome.
If one first commits an evil deed and later gives rise to a mind of regret, that [regret] is unwholesome in its cause, yet the regret itself is wholesome.

If, in a state of unwholesomeness, one does not first commit an evil deed but later gives rise to a mind of regret, that [regret] is unwholesome in its cause, and the regret itself is also unwholesome.
If one first performs a wholesome deed and later gives rise to a mind of regret, that [deed] is wholesome by reason of it, while the regret is unwholesome.
What is sleep? It is defined as a lack of mastery in mental activity, having the nature of obscurity and brevity.
Lack of mastery refers to causing the mind and its associates to function without autonomy; it is a derivative of delusion (*moha*).
Furthermore, because this [state] is by nature lacking mastery, it causes the mind and mental factors to become extremely dull and obscure.
These [factors] are of a wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate nature.
Their function is to serve as a basis for faults.
What is vitarka?
This refers to a specific form of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), characterized by mental verbalization and seeking, which has the nature of coarse conceptual discrimination.
"Mental verbalization" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which arises therein either based on reflection or based on wisdom.
Discerning gross characteristics refers to the investigation of gross characteristics such as those of jars, clothing, and vehicles.
Its function is to serve as the basis for pleasant contacts, painful contacts, and so forth.
What is sustained thought (*vicāra*)?

This refers to a specific form of wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), characterized by mental verbalization and investigation, which has the nature of discerning subtle characteristics within the mind.
"Subtle characteristics" refers to the meaning of discerning the distinctions between the formation and non-formation of subtle characteristics in things such as jars and garments.
What are the formations dissociated from mind?

They are conventionally designated based on the states of matter, mind, and so forth; that is, it is impossible to designate their nature as being either different or not different from those [states].

What, then, are these? They are: acquisition (*prāpti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the commonality of group (*nikāya-sabhāga*), birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), impermanence (*anityatā*), the collection of names (*nāma-kāya*), the collection of phrases (*pada-kāya*), the collection of phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*), and the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*). Such are these [factors].
How is it attained?
It means either to acquire or to accomplish.
This, moreover, is of three kinds: accomplishment of the seed, accomplishment of mastery, and accomplishment of manifest arising, as appropriate to each case.
What is the attainment of non-conception?

It is defined as the cessation of all non-permanent mental states and mental factors, preceded by the mental attention of the notion of renunciation, occurring when one is free from the defilements of the Sphere of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna) but not yet free from the defilements of the higher spheres.
What is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)?

It is defined as having already become free from the defilements of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and having further progressed beyond the first dhyāna, it has as its nature the cessation of all non-perpetually active mental states and a portion of the perpetually active mental states and mental factors, preceded by the mental attention that temporarily suspends perception.
Non-perpetually active refers to the six evolving consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ vijñānakāyāḥ*).
Perpetually active refers to the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*).
Among these, the cessation of the category of the six evolving consciousnesses and the afflicted mind constitutes the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
What is the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisattva*)?
It refers to the fruit obtained through the attainment of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
Having been born in that heaven, its nature consists in the cessation of all non-permanent mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
It is defined as the limit of duration for which one remains within a particular homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), as projected by prior karma.
What is the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*)?
It refers to the nature of all sentient beings, each of whom is characterized by similarity within their own respective class.
What is "birth"?
It refers to the nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within a particular homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*), which exist now though they did not previously exist.
What is aging?
It is characterized by the nature of the transformation and decay of the continuity of those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
What is duration?
It means that those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have the nature of continuing in a succession.
How are they impermanent?
It means that those conditioned phenomena have the nature of ceasing and perishing within that succession.
What is a name-group (nāmakāya)?
It has as its nature the metaphorical designation for the intrinsic nature of phenomena, such as when one speaks of "the eye" and so forth.
What is a phrase-group (padakāya)?
This refers to having the nature of being a designation for the distinctions among phenomena, such as when it is said that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," and so forth.
What is the "body of phonemes" (*vyañjana-kāya*)?
It refers to the individual syllables themselves, because these are able to express and clarify the nature of the former two [the body of names and the body of phrases].
It is also called "manifestation" (*vyañjana*), because it manifests the meaning as the basis for names and phrases.
It is also called "name" (*nāman*), because it does not shift into something else.
As for the former two natures, they refer to the expression of the self-nature and its specific distinctions.
"Manifestation" (khyāna) means "to make manifest" (prabhāvita).
What is the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*)?
It is defined as the state of not having attained the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*).
What is the aggregate of consciousness?
It is characterized by the discernment of objects.
It is also called "mind" (*citta*), because it is capable of accumulating [karmic impressions].
It is also called "mind" (*manas*), because it is subsumed under the category of mind.
If it is the most preeminent mind, it is the *ālayavijñāna*, for this is that which can collect the seeds of all formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, this mode of activity (*ākāra*) cannot be differentiated, because it proceeds as a continuous stream of a single type from beginning to end.

Moreover, when consciousness arises from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), or the heaven of non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) that discern objects arise again; because they proceed in dependence upon specific objective conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*), they repeatedly undergo interruption and then arise once more.
Furthermore, it is so called because it causes the cycle of birth and death to revolve and recur.
Regarding the *ālayavijñāna*: it is that which can store all seeds, and it can also store the manifestation of the conceit of "I"; moreover, it takes the body as its objective support (*ālambana*).
Furthermore, this is also called the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness), because it appropriates and maintains the body.

As for the "supreme manas," it refers to the consciousness that takes the *ālaya-vijñāna* as its object; it is constantly associated with self-delusion, self-view, self-pride, and self-love, persisting as a homogeneous continuity throughout successive moments, except during the state when the noble path of an Arhat or the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is present.
Thus, these six evolving consciousnesses, along with the afflicted manas and the ālayavijñāna—these eight are called the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha).
Question:
What is the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha)?
Answer:
"Accumulation" (skandha) is the meaning of *skandha*.
This is because it is a collective summary of the various categories of form and so forth, which exist as distinct types within the continuity of worldly existence.
As the Blessed One said: "Monks!

Whatever form there is—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; superior or inferior; near or far—all such forms, taken together as one, constitute the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha)."

Furthermore, there are twelve bases (āyatana), namely: the eye-base and the form-base; the ear-base and the sound-base; the nose-base and the odor-base; the tongue-base and the taste-base; the body-base and the tangible-base; the mind-base and the mental-object-base.
The five bases beginning with the eye, as well as the bases of visible form, sound, odor, and taste, have already been explained as before.
The base of tangibles refers to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and a portion of the tangible objects.
The mind base (*manāyatana*) is identical to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).

The sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) refers to the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, as well as unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and the various unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
What are the unconditioned phenomena?

They are the unconditioned space (*ākāśa-asaṃskṛta*), the unconditioned cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*), the unconditioned cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*), and suchness (*tathatā*), etc.
Space refers to that which accommodates and receives all forms.
Cessation not through deliberation refers to a cessation that is not dissociation from defilements.
What is meant by "not dissociation"?
It refers to the ultimate non-arising of the aggregates due to the absence of the antidote to the afflictions.
What is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)? It is that cessation which is dissociation (*visamyoga*).
What is disjunction?
It refers to the ultimate non-arising of the aggregates through the antidotes to the afflictions. What is suchness?
It refers to the dharma-nature and the selflessness of dharmas of all phenomena.
Question:
What is the meaning of "basis" (āyatana)?
Answer: The sense-bases (*āyatana*) have the meaning of being the gateways through which the various consciousnesses arise and grow.

Furthermore, there are the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), namely: the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible object element, and the body-consciousness element; and the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
The various elements (dhātus) of the eye and so forth, as well as the various elements of visible form and so forth, are as explained in the section on the bases (āyatanas).
As for the six consciousness elements (vijñāna-dhātu), their nature consists of the discernment [of objects] based upon the faculties such as the eye and conditioned by objects such as visible form.

The mind element (*manodhātu*) refers to those [mental states] that have just ceased in immediate succession; this is to clarify the support of the sixth consciousness and to establish the eighteen elements (*dhātus*) in detail.

Thus, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of ten bases (*āyatanas*), ten elements, and a portion of the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) consists of the mind base (*manāyatana*) and the seven mental elements. The remaining three aggregates, a portion of the aggregate of form, and all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) constitute the base of phenomena and the element of phenomena.
Question:
What is the meaning of "dhātu"?
Answer:
The meaning of *dhātu* (element) is the intrinsic characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of being devoid of functional activity (*nirvyāpāra*).
Question:
For what reason are the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) taught?
Answer:
It is for the sake of counteracting the three types of self-clinging, namely: clinging to a singular nature, clinging to a recipient, and clinging to an agent, respectively.
Furthermore, among these eighteen elements (dhātus), how many possess form?
They are ten elements and a portion of one, namely the intrinsic nature of the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
How many are formless?
This refers to the remaining elements.
How many are visible?
Only one: the element of form (*rūpadhātu*).
How many are non-visible?
They are the remaining elements.
How many are resistant?
This refers to the ten material elements (*rūpadhātu*), because they possess resistance (*sapratigha*) toward one another.
How many are non-resistant (*apratigha*)?
This refers to the remaining elements.
How many are with outflows (*sāsrava*)?
They are fifteen elements (*dhātu*) and a portion of the final three, because it is in these places that afflictions arise and because they are the domains of present activity.
How many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
This refers to a small portion of the final three [categories].
How many are bound to the desire realm? All of them.
How many are bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu)?
It is fourteen, excluding odor, taste, and the consciousnesses of nose and tongue.
How many are bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)?
This refers to the last three.
How many are unconditioned?
It refers to those very same [factors] that are untainted (*anāsrava*).
How many are subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*)?
That is to say, excluding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
How many are subsumed within the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*)?
That is to say, they are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
How many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate?

Ten are common to all three natures: the seven mental elements (*cittadhātu*), the element of form (*rūpadhātu*), the element of sound (*śabdadhātu*), and a portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*).
Regarding the eight neutral natures (*avyākṛta*),
how many are internal?
It is said to be twelve, excluding the elements of visible form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and the dharma-element.
How many are external?
They are the remaining six.
How many have an object?
This refers to the nature of the seven mind-elements and a portion of the dharma-element that consists of mental factors (*caitta*).
How many are without an object (*anālambana*)?
It refers to the remaining ten elements and a portion of the dharma-element.
How many are with conceptual discrimination?
They are the mental consciousness element, the mind element, and a portion of the phenomena element.
How many are appropriated?
This refers to the five internal elements and a portion of four elements, namely visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
How many are non-appropriated?
This refers to the remaining nine [elements] and a portion of the four [elements].
How many are sabhāga?
They are the five internal elements possessing form, because they share the same objective sphere as their respective consciousnesses.
How many are tatsabhāga?
This means that when one's own consciousness is empty, it is equal to its own kind.
*The Extensive Treatise on the Five Aggregates of the Mahāyāna*, Scroll One.
